title: SQL Querying & Joins: Quick Revision Notes
summary: Revision notes on reading data with SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT and NULL handling, the logical order a query runs in, and every join type from INNER to self joins.

chapters.title: SELECT Query Mental Model
points: SELECT picks columns, FROM names the table: SELECT name, city FROM users; avoid SELECT * in production code
A query describes the result you want; the engine chooses how to fetch it
Logical order: FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
Consequence of the order: a SELECT alias works in ORDER BY but not in WHERE
Result of every SELECT is a table of rows and columns, so it can feed another query as a subquery

chapters.title: Filtering, Sorting and Limiting
points: WHERE filters rows before grouping: WHERE age >= 18 AND city = 'Pune'
Operators: =, <>, IN (1,2,3), BETWEEN 10 AND 20 (inclusive both ends), LIKE 'A%' (% any chars, _ one char)
Precedence: AND binds tighter than OR, so use parentheses: WHERE a = 1 AND (b = 2 OR c = 3)
ORDER BY col DESC, col2 ASC sorts by multiple keys; without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20 pages results; LIMIT without ORDER BY returns arbitrary rows (SQL Server uses TOP, Oracle uses FETCH FIRST)

chapters.title: NULL Handling
points: NULL means unknown, not zero or empty string; any comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN
Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL; col = NULL never matches any row
WHERE keeps only rows that evaluate to TRUE, so UNKNOWN rows are dropped; NOT IN (list containing NULL) returns no rows
COALESCE(col, 'n/a') returns the first non-NULL argument; NULLIF(a, 0) returns NULL when a equals 0, avoiding divide-by-zero
Aggregates skip NULLs: COUNT(col) ignores them while COUNT(*) counts every row; ORDER BY NULL placement differs by engine (NULLS FIRST/LAST)

chapters.title: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT and FULL Joins
points: A join combines rows from two tables on a condition: FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id
INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides
LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows and fills right columns with NULL when there is no match; RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image
FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides (not supported in MySQL)
Find rows with no match: LEFT JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id WHERE b.a_id IS NULL (anti-join)

chapters.title: CROSS Joins, Self Joins and Join Mistakes
points: CROSS JOIN returns every pairing: m rows × n rows, with no ON clause; useful for generating combinations
Self join joins a table to itself with aliases: SELECT e.name, m.name AS manager FROM emp e LEFT JOIN emp m ON e.manager_id = m.id
Filtering the right table of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE turns it into an INNER JOIN; put that condition in ON instead
Joining on a non-unique key multiplies rows (one-to-many fan-out), which inflates COUNT and SUM
Forgetting the ON condition, or comma joins without WHERE, creates an accidental cross join

chapters.title: SQL Querying Cheat Sheet
points: Query order as written: SELECT → FROM → JOIN → WHERE → ORDER BY → LIMIT
Logical execution: FROM → WHERE → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
NULL tests: IS NULL, COALESCE(x, default), NOT IN breaks with NULLs, so prefer NOT EXISTS
Join table: INNER = matches only; LEFT = all left; RIGHT = all right; FULL = all both; CROSS = m×n
Pitfalls: SELECT *, missing ORDER BY with LIMIT, WHERE on the right side of a LEFT JOIN, duplicate rows after joining
